title: What is known about 1RB1LE_1LC0LF_1LA1RD_1LB0RD_0LC0LA_---1RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LE_1LC0LF_1LA1RD_1LB0RD_0LC0LA_---1RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.

It is a binary counter in disguise. At the left end a solid block of 1s grows by four cells per overflow, and each overflow comes about twice as many steps after the previous one. The rest of the tape is a word of blocks 1^k separated by 110 and runs of 10, which changes slowly. Around step 3.8·108 the word was used up and the run restarted with a longer one.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves no halt in the first 10,000 steps by the kernel alone and in the first 107 with native_decide; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1010 steps.

Where a halt would come from. The machine halts only in state F reading 0, and F is entered only from B reading 1 and stepping left (0LF). In the first 108 steps that happens 11,363,688 times and F always reads a 1.
What a proof needs. An exact description of one overflow and of the epoch change.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 420 cells have been visited and 244 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Overflows double
claims.text: At the times E is at the left end with the tape starting E>0 10 1^k 110, k grows by 4 from one time to the next (k = 83, 87, 91, 95, 99, 103) and the gaps double, to within a few hundred steps: 184,549,356, then 369,098,792, 738,197,896, 1,476,395,488 and 2,952,790,980 steps.

claims.title: An epoch change
claims.text: Width: 222 cells at 10<sup>7</sup> steps, 238 at 10<sup>8</sup>, 419 at 10<sup>9</sup>, 435 at 10<sup>10</sup>. The jump comes from a restart between steps 3.78·10<sup>8</sup> and 5.14·10<sup>8</sup>, when the left block is rebuilt and the tape grows by about 150 cells.

claims.title: F always reads 1
claims.text: F is entered only from B reading 1 (0LF); in the first 108 steps that happens 11,363,688 times and F reads a 1 every time.

claims.title: A run-length frame map, every case proved
claims.text: At every head turn write the tape as two lists of runs (blocks of equal cells), left and right of the head: a frame with list parameters. A table of 165 cases, each a pattern on the first few runs of both sides (lengths exact or at least 4, the rest of each side any list), sends each frame to the frame of the next head turn; every case is proved for all values of its parameters and all lists by one symbolic run (RLCase.sound), so the frame map next = rlNext cases is sound (rlNext_sound). Between two head turns this machine crosses only a few run boundaries, which is why a finite table covers a tape whose number of runs grows without bound.
claims.where: cases, lean/Cases.lean; the runs in lean/Pieces.lean; generated by py/frames.py lean with tools/py/bbtools/listframe.py; library tools/lean/TM/ListFrame.lean

claims.title: The frame map from blank tape
claims.text: The run from blank tape reaches the first frame (init_f0, kernel), and the frame map is defined for its first 100,000 frames (native_decide). If it is defined forever along this orbit, the machine never halts (no_halt_of_total).

claims.title: The case table covers the run
claims.text: Every frame at a head turn in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> steps (1,227,376 head turns) is matched by a case, and the case's next frame is the machine's (no mismatch, no unmatched frame); 161 cases at 10<sup>6</sup> steps, 165 at 3·10<sup>6</sup>, so a longer run may need more.

claims.title: No finite frame map with scalar parameters
claims.text: The frame-map method (stop at head turns, match the tape against finitely many templates with block-length parameters, fit affine cases) needs the tapes at head turns to fall into a bounded number of shapes. Here they do not: tokenizing the tape at every 7th head turn into maximal powers of words of length at most 4, the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps give 316,491 distinct shapes (exponents of 3 and more merged), 286,341 of them new in the last decade, and up to 52 tokens per tape; the number grows tenfold per decade of steps. For comparison the same count saturates at 32 shapes of at most 5 tokens for 1RB1LC_1LC1RD_1LA0LB_0RB1RE_1RF0RA_---0RC and at 89 for 1RB1RF_1LC1LF_0RE1LD_0LB1LD_---1RC_1RA0RD, where frame maps were proved. The cause is the counter itself: its digits form an arbitrary word, and the word of higher digits on the right grows too, so a frame needs a list parameter; the run-length frames above are such frames.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.133). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The run behaves like a binary counter in epochs; the increment and the epoch change have not been described exactly.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine runs a binary counter: every overflow takes twice as long as the last. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lists what is known.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Each overflow at the left end comes twice as many steps after the last.
The block at the left end grows by four cells per overflow.

sections.heading: A counter that doubles
html: Each time the head reaches the left end in state E with the tape reading E>0 1 0 1^k 1 1 0 …, the block 1^k has grown by four cells, and the time since the last such moment has doubled (to within a few hundred steps): overflows at steps 698,523,614, 883,072,970, 1,252,171,762, 1,990,369,658, 3,466,765,146 and 6,419,556,126, with k = 83, 87, 91, 95, 99, 103. So the tape grows like the logarithm of the time.

The rest of the tape is a word of blocks of 1s of odd length separated by 110 and runs of 10; it changes by a few cells per overflow, like the higher digits of a counter. When it has been worked through the run restarts on a larger scale. That happened between steps 3.78·108 and 5.14·108, the jump from 238 to 419 cells in the width.

sections.heading: What a halt would need
html: The only halting transition is F reading a 0. F is entered only when B reads a 1, writes a 0 and steps left; a halt needs a 0 there. In 108 steps that move happens 11,363,688 times and always lands on a 1.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.133). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 420 cells (349 left of the start, 50 right), with a density of 1s of 0.581.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A counter whose overflows at the left end double in time (the left block grows by 4 cells each); at step 3.8·10^8 it restarted on a larger scale.
